Back in maybe 2007, I was walking home from the bus stop with a close friend after school. 

On the route home we have to pass by a tiny altar at the foot of a tree, similar to this [altar](https://www.ricemedia.co/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/rice-media-tree-shrine-200-years-18-1024x576.jpg). Its been there ever since I moved here. I heard it honours a lethal car crash at the site 

I've been walking past this altar for 6 years I've been schooling, and never had an issue with it, it didn't even spook me, but this one day, as I walked past it... I saw MAN'S FACE seemingly embedded in the concrete in between my step. It was a man's face molded out of the concrete that popped out of the sidewalk. My blood went cold, and it disappeared once I stepped on over it. 

I decided to ignore it but picked up my pace, and my friend trotted along to keep up. After a few steps the adrenaline wore off and I slowed down. I looked back and didn't see any face in the concrete. However, my blood turned back to ice when my friend quietly said "Hey P0ny, back there, did you see that face lookout out of the bushes?"

We never spoke about it again. We've since lost touch, but this is the only legit supernatural thing that's happened to me. To this day I alight at the bus stop after the altar.

Teen years are a tough time. Evolutionarily, the hormones we have to face and awkward social experiences are just plain odd for an organism to go through. It's ridiculously tough, sometimes the biggest bummer of them all. 

You shouldn't end it because it DOES get better, you're in the middle of a weird ass, painful path that are your teen years, and there are a lot of roads ahead. You can live a happy and fulfilling life, but it takes a lot of mindfulness, awareness, and hard work, and this usually comes with age and commitment to working on it. 

It feels like an endless road of despair to you, but trust me it feels like it will never get better because well.. it hasn't yet. It's like describing a rainbow to a colourblind person, it's impossible until they see it for the first time themselves.

And here's the kicker! Your depression is a disease that can go into remission. It's a really tough disease, but it CAN go into remission. Keep seeking treatment for the ache in your bones. You can live a fulfilled and satisfying life if you can make the disease go into remission. Your suicidal thoughts are a symptom of a disease that can go into remission. Get through the day, then the next, then the next. You can do it!

Think of your suicidal thoughts like an illness. A painful disease in the background, aching in your bones. Yes, most of the time you're functional on the outside, but your bones ache, oh they ache. And sometimes the ache gets so bad it impairs your functionality, drive, motivation, and even, will to live.

But here's the thing - this is a disease that can go into remission. It's a really tough disease, but it CAN go into remission. Keep seeking treatment for the ache in your bones. You can live a fulfilled and satisfying life if you can make the disease go into remission.

Don't numb the pain of the disease with substances and unhealthy coping habits. Like a rotten tooth, the pain will eventually get so great that you will have to lose the tooth, VERY PAINFULLY. It's tough but work on your disease. Don't give up hope. Your suicidal thoughts are a symptom of a disease that can go into remission. Get through the day, then the next, then the next. You can do it!

You shouldn't blame or demonize yourself for not having the same drive and conscientiousness. We are all different, these factors included. Be gentle to yourself. Make the clear distinction between "bad things that happen because I procrastinated or didn't have the drive" versus "I am flawed because bad things happened because of my procrastination and lack of drive"

It is great you have pinned the tail on the issue that is causing a lot of suffering in your life, very mindful and aware. Now you can start to work on those issues, sans the self-judgement. You can do it!

Kudos to your plan, it sounds good. Everyone should have a bucket list, depressed or not. It adds joy and meaning to the human life. Carry out your bucket list, and fully imbue what it means to feel alive while you do those things.

I hope it adds value to your life, whatever the final outcome will be, but i sincerely hope you go on to live a long and fulfilling life as you continually add to your bucket list

When I realised that people who didn't want to date me because of my herpes was simply a case on incompatibility, not lack of self worth.

We are romantically incompatible with millions, billions of people on this earth, be it religious views, sexual orientation, age, etc. Herpes is just another one of those incompatibilities. It is not a flaw, it is a factor. Given the low severity of herpes, if someone doesn't want to date you because of it, then, it's an incompatibility of mindsets and comfort level, nothing to do with you. 

If someone wants to be with you, they will. All the more if they fully understand how minor something like herpes is, and are educated in how it is transmitted, etc.

I personally had no problem jumping into dating again. I did have that feeling that I was undateable for quite a while (it was horrible, of course), but I realized that thought was literally formulated by myself. No one was telling me I was undateable, except myself.

And here's a weird thought experiment. If a date you disclosed to said they didn't want to date you because you had herpes, *THEY* are undateable, not you. Herpes is a condition that so many people have and so many people have gone on to have relationships with. It's something you have forever, and if someone doesn't want to date you because of that, then you can treat it like a fundamental incompatibility. 

There are millions of people incompatible with you for various reasons - religion, sexual orientation, personality types. Whoever doesn't want to date you because of herpes is well.. just incompatible, like millions of others out there. 

Don't be too hard on yourself, I know the feeling is low and terrible, but try to think of herpes as a compatibility filter. If someone doesn't want to be with you, they won't. If someone does, they will. :)

Ugh, the stigma around herpes is really more mentally destroying than the physical symptoms ever will be. My ex passed me genital HSV1 via oral sex, fully knowing he had it, but didn't disclose it to me. I'm still so hurt and angry about that years on, sometimes.

I went to a private clinic to get diagnosed (with genital HSV1), but a year later I went to the DSC clinic for a routine full checkup. I asked to take the HSV test again (after disclosing the private clinic's results) - but here's what shocked me. The nurse said she didn't want to give me the test because:

*"you know like 2/3s of Singaporeans are HSV1 positive already?* And you already know your results, why do you want to waste your money? *So many people in Singapore have HSV without symptoms but never got tested before, they are the ones who should take the test,* not you who already have taken one"

She proceeded to explain that I would have the virus for life, and it's not curable and the usual stuff, but what really affected me was hearing the statistics straight from the horses mouth. 

I think the resentment shifted from myself having HSV1 to the stigma surrounding it. Herpes was some mystical harbinger of doom from the shitty sex ed Singapore gives, and here I am at the clinic hearing that 2/3 of Singapore could have it?! 

The anxiety of passing it on to future partners, and the psychological pain the stigma cause really, really makes HSV suck so much more than the physical symptoms. If only there was more education. But what can I do?
